title: Value Stream Mapping Analysis Skill with Lead Time, Takt and Bottleneck Check
summary: Skill that turns current-state value stream data into takt time, queue and lead time, value-added ratio, bottleneck load and a ranked list of flow improvements, with every number traceable to the input.
body:
---
name: vsm-analysis
description: Analyse current-state value stream map data. Use when someone shares process steps with cycle times, inventory or WIP, uptime and customer demand and wants lead time, bottleneck and improvement priorities.
---

# Skill: Value Stream Mapping Analysis

## Purpose
Take the numbers behind a current-state value stream map and compute what the drawing only suggests: takt time, queue time per step, total lead time, value-added ratio, the step closest to its limit, and where flow breaks. The skill proposes a ranked list of improvements, but every figure it reports must be traceable to the input.

## When to trigger
Use when a lean, operations or planning person pastes a step table, a map description or a spreadsheet extract and asks "where is the time going", "what is our lead time", "which step is the bottleneck" or "what should the future state look like". Do not use it to invent data for steps nobody measured.

## Where it runs
The text below can be stored as the instructions of a custom agent, as a reusable prompt, or as a skill file in a tool that supports skills. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism exists and what length limits apply. The skill does not need access to any system if the data is pasted in.

## Inputs
1. Customer demand per day (pieces) and available production time per day (seconds), after breaks and planned stops.
2. For each process step in flow order: name, cycle time per piece (seconds), uptime (percent), inventory or WIP waiting before the step (pieces), value-adding yes or no, batch size if relevant.
3. Optional: changeover time, number of operators, push or pull between steps, scrap or rework rate per step.
If demand or available time is missing, ask for it. Do not assume it.

## Procedure
1. Check the table. List missing fields and units. State the unit you will use for time (seconds) and for lead time (working days).
2. Takt time = available time per day divided by demand per day.
3. Effective cycle time per step = cycle time divided by uptime (as a fraction). Load vs takt = effective cycle time divided by takt. This assumes one station per step; divide by the number of parallel stations otherwise.
4. Queue time per step in days = WIP before the step divided by demand per day. Total queue = sum over steps.
5. Processing time = sum of cycle times. Lead time in days = total queue days plus (processing time in seconds divided by available seconds per day).
6. Value-added time = sum of cycle times of steps marked value-adding. Value-added ratio = value-added time divided by lead time in seconds (lead time days times available seconds per day).
7. Bottleneck = step with the highest effective cycle time. Report its load vs takt. A bottleneck at 75 percent of takt means capacity is not the main problem.
8. Find flow breaks: large queues, push between steps, batch steps, steps with uptime below the others, rework loops.
9. Propose improvements, each linked to one finding, with an expected effect on queue days (calculated, with the assumption written next to it). Typical levers: WIP limits or kanban between steps, supermarket instead of free queue, smaller batches, quick changeover, balancing work to takt.

## Output format
1. Key numbers table: takt, processing time, total queue days, lead time days, value-added time, value-added ratio, bottleneck and its load vs takt.
2. Step table: step, effective CT, load vs takt, queue days.
3. Findings (max 5), each with evidence from the table.
4. Improvement list, ranked by expected lead time effect, with assumptions.
5. Open questions and data gaps.

## Worked example (invented data)
Demand 80 pieces per day, available time 25,200 s per day, so takt = 315 s. Steps (cycle time s, uptime, WIP before): Saw 20, 95 percent, 640; CNC mill 210, 88 percent, 480; Deburr 90, 98 percent, 320; Inspect 120, 100 percent, 240; Pack 30, 100 percent, 80. Value-adding steps: Saw and CNC mill.
- Queue days: 8 + 6 + 4 + 3 + 1 = 22 days.
- Processing time: 470 s. Lead time = 22 + 470 / 25,200 = 22.02 days.
- Value-added time 230 s, so value-added ratio = 230 / (22.02 x 25,200) = 0.041 percent.
- Effective CT: CNC mill 238.6 s is the highest, load vs takt 75.8 percent. Inspect 120 s is 38.1 percent.
- Finding: the line is not capacity-limited. Almost all lead time is waiting. If WIP before each step is limited to one day of demand (80 pieces, an assumption to be confirmed by the team), queue becomes 5 days and lead time about 5.02 days, a 77 percent reduction.

## Pitfalls
- Mixing units: WIP in pieces, demand in lots, cycle time in minutes. Convert first and say so.
- Treating the average WIP of one day as a constant. Ask for the range, especially before shared resources.
- Calling inspection or paperwork "value-adding" because the customer requires it. Mark it as necessary non-value-adding and keep it out of the value-added time.
- Reporting a value-added ratio to two decimals as if it were precise. It is an order of magnitude.
- In aviation and other regulated work, a required inspection or release step is never a candidate for removal by this skill. Only waiting around it can be discussed, and quality or certifying staff decide.

## Adapting to your environment
Change the unit of lead time if you work in shifts. Add a column for changeover time if the product mix is wide. If your plant uses a different value-added definition, put it in the inputs section so the skill uses yours.

## Data protection and safety
Process data is usually not personal data. If the input contains operator names or individual performance, remove them or involve the works council or data protection officer before using a cloud AI service. Do not paste customer-confidential drawings or part numbers unless your policy allows it. The skill output is an analysis for a team workshop and not an approved process change.

title: OEE Loss Analysis Skill that Converts Shift Data into a Minutes-Based Loss Waterfall
summary: Skill that takes shift data and loss categories, calculates availability, performance, quality and OEE, and converts every loss into minutes so the team sees which loss to attack first.
body:
---
name: oee-loss-analysis
description: Calculate OEE from shift data and turn each loss into minutes of planned production time. Use when someone has downtime, speed and scrap numbers and wants to know which loss to reduce first.
---

# Skill: OEE Loss Analysis

## Purpose
OEE as a single percentage hides where the time went. This skill calculates availability, performance, quality and OEE, then expresses every loss in minutes of planned production time. The result is a waterfall: planned time, availability losses, speed losses, quality losses, fully productive time. A team can discuss minutes; it is harder to discuss percentages.

## When to trigger
Use when someone shares shift or day data for one machine or line and asks for OEE, "why is OEE low", "what are our biggest losses" or "what is a point of OEE worth". Do not use it to compare machines with different definitions of planned time unless the definition is stated.

## Where it runs
As instructions of a custom agent, a reusable prompt or a skill file. It works on pasted data. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism and length limits apply.

## Inputs
1. Planned production time (minutes) for the period. State what is excluded (breaks, planned maintenance, no-demand time). The definition must be agreed in the plant and written down.
2. Downtime events with minutes and reason, split into breakdowns and changeovers or setups.
3. Ideal cycle time per part (seconds). Ask where it comes from: design speed, best demonstrated speed, or standard.
4. Total parts produced and good parts.
5. Optional: reason codes for minor stops, rework counts, startup rejects.

## Procedure
1. Run time = planned time minus downtime (breakdowns and changeovers).
2. Availability = run time / planned time.
3. Ideal time = total parts x ideal cycle time / 60 (minutes). Performance = ideal time / run time. If performance is above 100 percent, stop and flag the ideal cycle time as wrong or the counts as inconsistent.
4. Quality = good parts / total parts. Good time = good parts x ideal cycle time / 60.
5. OEE = availability x performance x quality. Cross-check: OEE = good time / planned time. If the two differ, find the error before reporting.
6. Loss waterfall in minutes: breakdowns, changeovers, speed and minor stops (run time minus ideal time), rejects (ideal time minus good time). The remainder is fully productive time.
7. Rank the losses by minutes. Express each loss as share of planned time.
8. For the largest loss propose two or three analysis steps (not solutions): for example a Pareto of the breakdown reasons, a changeover video, a minor-stop count with a stopwatch for two shifts.

## Output format
1. Key figures: A, P, Q, OEE and the cross-check.
2. Loss table: loss, minutes, share of planned time, rank.
3. One-sentence reading of the biggest loss.
4. Data quality notes (missing reasons, suspicious values).
5. Next analysis steps (max 3).

## Worked example (invented data)
Planned time 420 min. Breakdowns 35 min, changeovers 40 min. Ideal cycle time 30 s. Total parts 600, good parts 582.
- Run time = 420 - 35 - 40 = 345 min. Availability = 345 / 420 = 82.1 percent.
- Ideal time = 600 x 30 / 60 = 300 min. Performance = 300 / 345 = 87.0 percent.
- Quality = 582 / 600 = 97.0 percent.
- OEE = 0.8214 x 0.8696 x 0.97 = 69.3 percent. Cross-check: good time = 582 x 30 / 60 = 291 min, 291 / 420 = 69.3 percent.
- Waterfall: breakdowns 35 min (8.3 percent of planned), changeovers 40 min (9.5 percent), speed and minor stops 45 min (10.7 percent), rejects 9 min (2.1 percent), fully productive 291 min (69.3 percent). Total 420 min (the percentages add to 99.9 because of rounding).
- Reading: speed and minor stops are the largest single loss, bigger than breakdowns. Without minor-stop data the team would have chased breakdowns first.

## Pitfalls
- Changing the ideal cycle time to make OEE look better. Keep one reference and document it.
- Averaging OEE values of shifts with different planned times. Add the minutes and parts first, then calculate.
- Counting planned maintenance as a loss in one plant and not in another, then comparing plants.
- Treating 85 percent as a universal target. Targets depend on process and definition. Do not state one unless the user gives it.
- Including parts reworked later as good parts. Decide the rule and apply it the same way every shift.

## Adapting to your environment
Add reason-code columns if your MES or machine data provides them. If you also track time outside the planned production time, state the extended definition explicitly and keep the two metrics apart. Match category names to those on your shopfloor board.

## Data protection and safety
Machine data is usually not personal data, but shift reports may name operators. Remove names and compare machines and shifts, not people. If shift-level data could be used for performance assessment of individuals, involve the works council before using it with an AI service. In aviation production, scrap and rework records belong to the quality system; the skill output is analysis and does not replace nonconformance handling.

title: 5S Audit Scoring Skill that Turns Audit Notes into Evidence-Based Scores and Actions
summary: Skill that converts 5S audit notes and photo descriptions into scores per S with the evidence for each, a trend against the last audit and a short owner-based action list without blame.
body:
---
name: five-s-audit-scoring
description: Score a 5S audit from the auditor's notes. Use when someone pastes observations for an area and wants consistent scores per S, evidence, trend and actions.
---

# Skill: 5S Audit Scoring

## Purpose
Different auditors give different scores for the same area. This skill applies one scoring rule to the auditor's observations, shows the evidence behind each score and produces a short action list. It supports the audit; it does not replace walking the area.

## When to trigger
Use when someone shares audit notes, a checklist with comments or photo descriptions for one area and asks for scores, a summary for the area board, or a comparison with the previous audit.

## Where it runs
As instructions of a custom agent, a reusable prompt or a skill file. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism and length limits apply.

## Inputs
1. Area name and audit date.
2. Observations per S: Sort (unneeded items), Set in order (places, markings, shadow boards), Shine (cleanliness, sources of dirt), Standardise (visual standards, checklists, responsibilities), Sustain (audit rhythm, follow-up, discipline).
3. Scoring scale. Default: 0 to 4 per question, with 0 = not in place, 2 = partly in place, 4 = in place and held at the last three audits. Use the plant's own scale if there is one.
4. Optional: previous scores and open actions.

## Procedure
1. Split the notes into questions per S, normally three. If the notes do not cover an S, write "not observed" and do not score it.
2. Score each question with the scale. Quote the observation that supports the score. If there is no evidence for a high score, score lower or ask.
3. Score per S = sum of question scores / (4 x number of questions), as a percentage.
4. Area score = average of the five S, equal weights unless the plant defines weights. State which.
5. Compare with the previous audit: change in points per S and overall. Do not interpret a change of a few points as a trend from one comparison.
6. Draft actions: one per finding with a score of 2 or less, each with a suggested owner role (not a person), a due date proposal and how the result will be seen. Limit to five actions.
7. Check wording: describe the situation, not the person. No "careless", no "lazy".

## Output format
1. Area, date, auditor.
2. Table: S, question, score, evidence.
3. Scores per S and area score, change against previous audit.
4. Actions (max 5): finding, action, owner role, due date, evidence of completion.
5. One sentence for the area board.

## Worked example (invented data)
Area: tool crib. Three questions per S, scores 0 to 4.
- Sort 3, 3, 4 = 10 of 12 = 83.3 percent. Set in order 4, 3, 3 = 10 of 12 = 83.3 percent. Shine 2, 3, 2 = 7 of 12 = 58.3 percent. Standardise 2, 1, 2 = 5 of 12 = 41.7 percent. Sustain 1, 2, 1 = 4 of 12 = 33.3 percent.
- Area score = (10 + 10 + 7 + 5 + 4) / 60 = 36 / 60 = 60.0 percent. Previous audit 31 of 60 = 51.7 percent, change +8.3 points.
- Reading: the physical S (Sort, Set in order) are strong, the system S (Standardise, Sustain) are weak. This is a typical pattern: an area can look tidy while no system holds it there. The audit notes, not the score alone, show whether that is the case.
- Action example: Standardise score 1 on "visual standard for the return place of calibrated tools". Action: one photo standard at the return shelf. Owner role: area supervisor. Due: next audit. Evidence: photo on the area board.

## Pitfalls
- Scoring what is easy to see (cleanliness) and skipping the audit rhythm. Sustain is about the system, not a clean floor.
- Letting the person who works in the area score it alone. Rotate auditors.
- Using scores to rank people or shifts. Rank problems, not people.
- Photos showing faces or names on badges. Frame the photo on the item.
- Treating 5S as a replacement for tool control, FOD prevention, calibration control or safety inspection. In aviation maintenance those have their own procedures and records.

## Adapting to your environment
Replace the three default questions per S with your plant's checklist. If you use a 1 to 5 scale, change the denominator in the S score. Add an "evidence" column if your auditors take photos.

## Data protection and safety
Audit notes can mention names. Replace them with role names before processing. Check whether photos taken in the area are allowed by the site rules and whether the works council has agreed to the audit process. Do not paste notes with safety incidents into a general-purpose AI service without checking company policy.

title: A3 Coaching Skill that Challenges Problem Statements, Cause Chains and Countermeasures
summary: Skill that acts as an A3 coach: asks one question at a time, tests whether the goal is measurable, the cause chain holds and the countermeasures cover the gap, and scores the A3 against a simple rubric.
body:
---
name: a3-coaching
description: Coach the author of an A3 problem-solving report. Use when someone shares a draft A3 or a problem and wants questions and a review, not a finished A3 written for them.
---

# Skill: A3 Coaching

## Purpose
An A3 is a thinking tool. A coach does not write it for the author; the coach asks questions until the logic holds. This skill plays that role: it reviews each section, asks the next useful question, and checks that goal, causes and countermeasures fit together with numbers.

## When to trigger
Use when someone shares a draft A3 (background, current condition, goal, root cause analysis, countermeasures, plan, follow-up) or a rough problem description. Do not use it to produce a complete A3 from nothing. If the user insists, produce a skeleton with questions in each box and say so.

## Where it runs
As instructions of a custom agent, a reusable prompt or a skill file. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism and length limits apply.

## Inputs
1. The A3 draft or a free-text problem description.
2. Data the author has: counts, dates, a Pareto, measurements. If there are no numbers, the first coaching question is where numbers can be found.
3. Optional: who owns the process, deadline and the area the A3 covers.

## Rules of the coach
1. One question at a time, at most three if the user asks for a full review.
2. No solutions before the cause chain is checked. If the author proposes a solution early, ask which cause it removes.
3. Praise only specific things ("the goal has a baseline and a date"), never generally.
4. Every statement in the review quotes the A3 text it refers to.

## Procedure
1. Background and problem: is it one problem, observable, in one place and period? Is the gap shown as baseline versus target?
2. Goal: measurable, with unit, baseline, target and date? Compute the gap in absolute terms.
3. Current condition: based on data from the process, not opinion? Is the biggest contributor identified (Pareto or similar)?
4. Cause chain (5 Why or fishbone): read each link backwards with "therefore". If a link does not hold, ask for evidence. Is the last cause something the team can act on? Was each cause checked at the place of work?
5. Countermeasures: does each map to one cause? Compute whether their expected effect covers the gap. If the author has no expected effect, ask for an estimate.
6. Plan: owners as roles or names agreed by the author, dates, one check date for the effect.
7. Follow-up: how will the result be measured, by whom, and what happens if the target is missed?
8. Score the A3 with the rubric below and list the one section to improve first.

## Rubric
Seven sections, 0 = missing, 1 = present but weak, 2 = solid. Maximum 14. Use it as a conversation aid, not as a grade for people.

## Output format
1. Section review: one line per section with the quoted text and your observation. Ask questions only for the weakest section (at most three in a full review, following the rules of the coach).
2. Numbers check: gap, expected effect of countermeasures, remaining gap.
3. Rubric score and the single section to work on next.
4. The next question to the author.

## Worked example (invented data)
Draft: "Scrap on the milling cell is too high. Goal: reduce scrap to 2.0 percent by end of quarter." Data: 12,000 parts in four weeks, 504 scrapped.
- Baseline 504 / 12,000 = 4.2 percent. Target 2.0 percent means at most 240 scrap parts at the same volume. Gap 264 parts, a 52 percent reduction.
- Pareto of scrap causes: edge burrs 210 (41.7 percent), wrong offset 140 (27.8 percent), tool wear 84 (16.7 percent), handling 40 (7.9 percent), material 30 (6.0 percent).
- The author plans countermeasures for burrs and offsets and expects 70 percent less for each. Expected effect = 0.7 x (210 + 140) = 245 parts. Remaining scrap = 504 - 245 = 259 parts = 2.16 percent. The goal is not reached.
- Coach question: "Your two countermeasures remove about 245 parts, the gap is 264. What closes the remaining 19 parts, or does the goal need a different date?" Adding tool wear at the same 70 percent gives 304 parts removed and 1.67 percent.
- Rubric: goal 2, current condition 2, cause chain 1 (burr cause not verified at the machine), countermeasures 1, plan 1, follow-up 0, background 2 = 9 of 14. Next section to improve: follow-up.

## Pitfalls
- The coach writes the content and the author learns nothing. Ask, do not tell.
- Accepting "operator error" as a root cause. Ask what in the process makes the error likely.
- Goals without a baseline or date.
- Rubric points used to compare authors. Use them to guide one conversation.
- Safety, quality or regulatory findings in an A3 (for example a nonconformance in aviation production) follow their own procedures. The A3 does not replace corrective action records.

## Adapting to your environment
Match the section names to your company A3 template. Add a "customer impact" section if your template has one. If your A3 uses a fishbone instead of 5 Why, keep step 4 but test each branch.

## Data protection and safety
A3s may contain names, customer data or incident details. Replace names with roles. Do not paste customer-confidential or export-controlled data into a general-purpose AI service without checking your policy. Involve the works council if A3 data are used to assess individuals.

title: Gemba Walk Planning and Follow-up Skill with Observation Questions and Action Tracking
summary: Skill that prepares a focused gemba walk with a theme, a time budget, respectful questions and a capture sheet, then turns the notes into actions with owners and a follow-up closure rate.
body:
---
name: gemba-walk-planner
description: Plan a gemba walk and process its notes. Use when a manager or lean coach wants a focused route, questions to ask at each stop, and an action list after the walk.
---

# Skill: Gemba Walk Planning and Follow-up

## Purpose
A gemba walk is going to the place where the work is done to understand the process and support the people doing it. Walks often fail for two reasons: no focus, and no follow-up. This skill prepares a short focused walk and, afterwards, turns the notes into actions with owners and a closure check.

## When to trigger
Use when someone says they will walk an area (production cell, goods-in, line maintenance bay, stores, quality inspection) and asks what to look at and ask, or after the walk when they paste notes. Do not use it to produce audit findings about individuals.

## Where it runs
As instructions of a custom agent, a reusable prompt or a skill file. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism and length limits apply.

## Inputs
1. Area, time available (minutes) and who walks.
2. Theme for this walk. One theme only, for example safety, flow of material, standard work, quality at the source, visual management.
3. Last walk's open actions and the area's key numbers (for example the SQDC board).
4. After the walk: the raw notes.

## Procedure before the walk
1. Fix the theme and write one sentence on what "good" looks like for this theme in this area.
2. Time budget: 5 minutes preparation, 5 minutes debrief with the area lead, the rest split evenly over the stops. Choose the number of stops so each has at least 5 minutes.
3. Route: stops in process order, not in order of convenience. Include the board, one process step and one place where material or information waits.
4. Questions per stop, open and about the process: "Show me how you do this step." "What gets in the way here?" "What happens when this goes wrong?" "How do you know you did it right?" Add one question about last week's action.
5. Rules: do not fix things on the spot, do not give instructions to operators, do not take photos of people without asking, thank people.

## Procedure after the walk
1. Sort the notes into observations (what was seen), questions that remain open, and ideas. Observations must be facts, not judgements.
2. Create actions only for items the area lead agrees with. Each action: what, owner (a role or an agreed name), due date, how it will be seen.
3. Mark safety findings for immediate handling through the normal safety process. Do not park them in an action list.
4. Calculate the closure rate of actions from the last walks: closed divided by opened.

## Output format
Before: theme, definition of good, time plan, route with questions, rules.
After: observation list, open questions, action table (action, owner, due, evidence), closure rate, one sentence to give back to the team.

## Worked example (invented data)
Walk of 30 minutes in a machining cell, theme: flow of material.
- Budget: 5 minutes preparation, 5 minutes debrief, 20 minutes for 4 stops = 5 minutes per stop. Stops: material supermarket, machine 1, inspection table, outgoing rack.
- Question at the inspection table: "Show me what happens when a part waits here for release." Observation: 6 parts waiting, oldest part 2 shifts old.
- Closure rate over the last four walks: 12 actions opened, 9 closed, 3 open. Closure rate = 9 / 12 = 75 percent. The three open actions are reviewed first at the next walk before new ones are added.
- Feedback sentence: "We saw that parts wait for inspection release; we agreed one action on how release requests are signalled."

## Pitfalls
- Walking without a theme and writing 30 observations nobody follows.
- Asking "why did you do that" in a way that sounds like blame. Ask "what makes this step difficult".
- Creating actions for the area without the area lead agreeing.
- Skipping the closure review. Without it the walks lose credibility within weeks.
- In aviation maintenance, a gemba walk is not an audit of airworthiness work and does not replace compliance monitoring. Do not instruct anyone to deviate from approved data during a walk.

## Adapting to your environment
Use your plant's theme list. If you work in shifts, add a night walk each quarter. Align the action table with your tracking tool (a list or a task board) so the skill output can be pasted in.

## Data protection and safety
Notes may contain names or personal remarks. Use roles. Check with the works council how walk notes may be used; they must not become individual performance records. Do not paste confidential customer information into a general-purpose AI service.

title: Downtime Pareto Analysis Skill with Minutes, Frequency and Average Duration Views
summary: Skill that cleans a downtime log, builds a Pareto by minutes and by event count, adds average duration per cause and recommends which cause deserves which kind of analysis next.
body:
---
name: downtime-pareto
description: Build a downtime Pareto from a log of stops. Use when someone has reason codes with minutes and counts and wants to know which causes to attack and how.
---

# Skill: Downtime Pareto Analysis

## Purpose
A Pareto by minutes alone hides micro stops that happen many times, and a Pareto by count alone hides rare long breakdowns. This skill builds both views, adds the average duration per event and recommends the type of analysis each cause needs, so the team picks the right tool: setup reduction, autonomous maintenance, root cause analysis or better logging.

## When to trigger
Use when someone pastes or attaches a downtime export (reason, minutes, optionally date, machine, count) and asks for a Pareto, "what are our top losses" or "where should the maintenance team start".

## Where it runs
As instructions of a custom agent, a reusable prompt or a skill file. For long exports use a tool that can run code or a spreadsheet; do not let a language model add up hundreds of rows by itself. Check in your tenant or tool documentation which mechanism and limits apply.

## Inputs
1. Log rows: reason code or text, duration in minutes, one row per event or one row per reason with a count.
2. Period and machine or line, and the planned production time for the period.
3. Optional: the plant's reason-code list and its definition of a minor stop.

## Procedure
1. Check units and the period. Reject rows with negative or empty durations and list them.
2. Merge reason names that mean the same thing (for example "tool broke" and "tool breakage"), and list every merge so the user can undo it.
3. Aggregate per reason: total minutes, number of events, average minutes per event = total / events.
4. Sort by total minutes descending, but put "Other" at the end. Compute share and cumulative share.
5. If "Other" is more than about 10 percent of minutes, say that the reason codes are too coarse and suggest recoding before analysis.
6. Second view: rank by event count. A reason with high count and low average is a minor-stop problem. A reason with low count and high average is a breakdown or setup problem.
7. For each of the top causes recommend the next analysis: high minutes and long average = root cause analysis or maintenance review; high count and short average = observation and stopwatch study, sensor or feeder check; changeover = changeover analysis; waiting for people or material = flow and logistics check.
8. Convert the top cause to planned production time: minutes / planned time.

## Output format
1. Pareto table: rank, reason, minutes, events, average minutes, share, cumulative share.
2. Second table sorted by events (top 5).
3. Reading in three sentences.
4. Recommended next analysis per top cause.
5. Data quality notes and merges made.

## Worked example (invented data)
Four weeks, one line, 112 events, 1,640 minutes in total. Planned production time over the period: 8,400 minutes (invented).
- Changeover 540 min, 18 events, 30.0 min average, 32.9 percent.
- Material shortage 310 min, 22 events, 14.1 average, 18.9 percent, cumulative 51.8 percent.
- Tool breakage 280 min, 9 events, 31.1 average, 17.1 percent, cumulative 68.9 percent.
- Sensor fault 190 min, 31 events, 6.1 average, 11.6 percent, cumulative 80.5 percent.
- Program error 120 min, 6 events, 20.0 average, 7.3 percent, cumulative 87.8 percent.
- Waiting for QA release 95 min, 12 events, 7.9 average, 5.8 percent, cumulative 93.6 percent.
- Cleaning 40 min, 4 events, 10.0 average, 2.4 percent, cumulative 96.0 percent. Other 65 min, 10 events, 6.5 average, 4.0 percent, cumulative 100 percent.
- Reading: four causes make 80.5 percent of the minutes, which is a rule of thumb, not a law. Sensor fault is only fourth in minutes but first in events (31) with 6.1 minutes each: a minor-stop problem that a stopwatch and a look at the sensor will clarify. Changeover alone is 540 / 8,400 = 6.4 percent of planned time.

## Pitfalls
- Trusting reason codes that operators pick to end the stop quickly. Spot-check a sample against what was seen at the machine.
- Comparing causes in different periods or machines without saying so.
- Ignoring stops below the logging threshold. If micro stops are not logged, the Pareto cannot show them.
- Treating the cumulative 80 percent line as a target. It is only a way to find where to start.
- For aircraft or safety-critical equipment, a downtime reason such as a failed inspection or a quality hold must not be "optimised away". Reduce the waiting, not the control.

## Adapting to your environment
Use the plant's reason-code list and map free text to it. If you work with a Power BI or Fabric model, use the skill for interpretation and let the model do the aggregation. Add a filter by shift if the pattern differs between shifts, but see the data protection note.

## Data protection and safety
Downtime logs are usually not personal data, but free-text reasons sometimes name people. Strip names before analysis. Do not use shift-level results to judge individual operators; involve the works council if logs could be used that way.
